helpText: VAR here reviews goals and penalties only, and you only see a review that changed the call. A goal that is ruled out adds no score, scorer or shot stats. A foul the referee missed can become a penalty, and that kick can go in, be saved or miss.
VAR example: At 0-0 a goal goes to a review and is ruled out. It stays 0-0 and nobody gets a goal. If a review gives a penalty and the kick misses, it still stays 0-0.

help.text: 📺 VAR, where real football uses it. From 2026 on, a match can go to a video review, but only in a competition that two sources confirm uses VAR in 2026/27. Right now that is: Premier League, La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga, Champions League. Every other league and every domestic cup plays without it until it has been confirmed the same way. In real football a review can look at goals, penalty calls, straight red cards and a card shown to the wrong player, and the referee's call stands unless it was a clear and obvious error. This game reviews goals and penalties only. A goal that is ruled out counts for nothing: no score, no scorer, no shot on the stats. A foul the referee missed can become a penalty, and the kick is a real one that can go in, be saved or miss. You only see a review that changed the call, and it is rare. The numbers come from published counts of real seasons, and we took the lowest: a goal ruled out about once in 13 matches, a penalty given about once in 15. It works both ways, for you and against you, and it does change results. Example: it is 0-0, a goal is ruled out, then a penalty a review gave is missed. It stays 0-0. Each decision is made once and saved with the match, so the live match and the full time report always agree. Open the match's ? button to read this again.
